Abstract:  
Medical imaging plays a pivotal role in early disease detection, surgical planning, and post-treatment monitoring. Among various 
imaging modalities, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT) are widely used due to their 
complementary strengths MRI offers superior soft tissue contrast, while CT excels in visualizing dense structures like bones. 
However, relying on a single modality often limits diagnostic precision, especially in complex clinical cases such as brain tumors, 
stroke evaluation, and orthopedic planning. Consequently, fusing information from both MRI and CT images into a unified 
representation, known as multi-modal image fusion, has become an essential approach to enhance diagnostic accuracy and clinical 
decision-making. 
Traditional image fusion techniques, including wavelet transforms, PCA, and Laplacian pyramids, have demonstrated limited 
performance due to their reliance on handcrafted features and linear transformations. These methods often result in loss of critical 
structural or functional information. The rise of deep learning, particularly Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and 
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), has revolutionized image processing by enabling the automatic extraction and synthesis of 
complex features across domains. These generative models not only learn hierarchical representations from data but also preserve 
the contextual integrity of both modalities during the fusion process. GANs have shown exceptional capability in generating 
realistic, high-resolution images, while VAEs offer probabilistic latent space modeling that is beneficial for uncertainty estimation 
in medical contexts. 
This study proposes and evaluates a multi-modal image fusion framework leveraging GAN and VAE architectures to combine 
MRI and CT images for enhanced medical diagnosis. The research utilizes multiple publicly available datasets (e.g., TCIA, BraTS), 
implements both pixel-level and feature-level fusion strategies, and conducts extensive evaluations using quantitative metrics such 
as Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and classification accuracy for downstream diagnostic 
tasks. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed GAN- and VAE-based fusion models significantly outperform 
traditional fusion techniques in terms of visual clarity, preservation of diagnostic details, and computational efficiency. Moreover, 
a comprehensive benchmark of different model variants (Pix2Pix, CycleGAN, β-VAE, CVAE-GAN) is provided to guide future 
research and clinical implementation. This work contributes to the field by offering a reproducible framework, open-source 
implementation, and actionable insights for integrating deep generative models into radiological workflows, thereby paving the way 
for AI-augmented precision diagnostics.

1.1. 
Background: Importance of Imaging in Medical

cardiovascular disorders, and neurodegenerative illnesses

outcomes and reducing healthcare costs. In this context, 
medical imaging serves as the first and often the most 
informative step in the clinical decision-making pipeline.

1.2. 
 Modalities Overview: MRI and CT – A 
Comparative Lens 
Among the many available imaging modalities, Magnetic 
Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography 
(CT) are two of the most widely used and clinically powerful 
technologies. Each has its own strengths, weaknesses, and 
application domains: 
A. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) 
MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses to 
generate detailed images of internal body structures, especially 
soft tissues such as the brain, muscles, spinal cord, and internal 
organs. MRI is renowned for its excellent contrast resolution, 
allowing the differentiation of subtle tissue variations. It is 
particularly valuable in neurological imaging, musculoskeletal 
examinations, and cardiac diagnostics. 
❖ Advantages: Superior soft tissue contrast, non-ionizing 
radiation, multi-planar capabilities. 
❖ Limitations: 
Longer 
scan 
times, 
high 
cost, 
contraindications in patients with metallic implants or 
pacemakers. 
B. Computed Tomography (CT) 
CT scans use X-rays to produce cross-sectional images of the 
body and are particularly effective at imaging dense tissues 
such as bones and calcifications. CT offers high spatial 
resolution and rapid imaging, making it suitable for emergency 
situations like trauma or hemorrhage. 
❖ Advantages: 
Rapid 
image 
acquisition, 
superior 
visualization of bone structures, widespread availability. 
❖ Limitations: Ionizing radiation exposure, lower soft tissue 
contrast compared to MRI. 
Complementarity 
While MRI is excellent at distinguishing soft tissues and 
pathological anomalies, CT excels at visualizing structural and 
bony details. Hence, many complex clinical cases, such as brain 
tumor resection planning or spinal cord injury assessment, 
require both modalities. When evaluated in isolation, neither 
MRI nor CT provides a complete picture. Therefore, multi-
modal 
image 
fusion 
becomes 
imperative 
to 
obtain 
comprehensive and clinically actionable insights. 
1.3. 
 The 
Necessity 
of 
Fusion: 
Integrating 
Complementary Data 
Multi-modal image fusion refers to the process of integrating 
information from two or more imaging sources into a single, 
unified image that retains the essential features of each input. 
The objective is to enhance the interpretability and usefulness 
of the image in clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. In 
medical practice, the fusion of MRI and CT images provides a 
synergistic view of both soft and hard tissues, offering a richer, 
more informative diagnostic tool. 
This fusion process is particularly vital in the following clinical 
scenarios: 
❖ Neurosurgery: Fused MRI-CT images help identify tumor 
boundaries while simultaneously mapping their spatial 
relation to skull structures or blood vessels. 
❖ Radiation 
Therapy 
Planning: 
Accurate 
tissue 
characterization enables precise targeting of radiation 
doses, reducing harm to healthy tissue. 
❖ Orthopedic Surgery: CT reveals bone detail, while MRI 
provides insight into cartilage, ligaments, and bone 
marrow. 
❖ Oncology: Fusion enhances tumor delineation, staging, 
and monitoring post-treatment progression or recurrence. 
Despite its potential, traditional fusion approaches such as 
Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Wavelet Transforms, 
and Laplacian Pyramids often fall short. These classical 
methods typically operate at the pixel or feature level using 
fixed mathematical rules. They may introduce artifacts, lose 
diagnostic information, and lack the adaptability needed for 
complex medical data. In contrast, data-driven approaches like 
deep learning offer the ability to learn optimal fusion 
strategies directly from data, making them more flexible and 
powerful. 
1.4. 
Deep Learning and the Rise of Generative Models 
in Medical Imaging 
In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a transformative 
technology in medical imaging. Powered by advances in 
computational hardware, large annotated datasets, and open-
source frameworks, deep learning models have surpassed 
traditional machine learning methods in tasks such as 
segmentation, classification, registration, and synthesis. 
Among the most promising areas of application is image fusion 
using deep generative models, specifically Generative 
Adversarial 
Networks 
(GANs) 
and 
Variational 
Autoencoders (VAEs). 
❖ Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs): Introduced 
by Goodfellow et al. in 2014, GANs consist of two 
competing networks—a generator and a discriminator—
that engage in a minimax game. The generator attempts to 
produce realistic images, while the discriminator evaluates 
their authenticity. Over iterative training, the generator 
learns to synthesize data that closely approximates the real 
distribution. GANs have been widely applied in medical 
imaging for: 
▪ 
Cross-modality synthesis (e.g., MRI-to-CT translation) 
▪ 
Image super-resolution 
▪ 
Noise reduction and inpainting 
❖ Variational 
Autoencoders 
(VAEs): 
VAEs 
are 
probabilistic generative models that learn a compressed 
latent representation of input data and reconstruct it 
through sampling from a learned distribution. Unlike 
GANs, VAEs provide explicit control over the latent space 
and can model uncertainty, making them valuable in 
clinical settings where interpretability and reliability are 
crucial.

1.5. 
 Research Objectives and Significance 
The primary goal of this research is to explore, design, and 
evaluate deep generative models for fusing MRI and CT 
images, 
with an emphasis on improving diagnostic 
interpretability and clinical accuracy. While prior works have 
applied GANs or VAEs in isolated scenarios, few studies have 
conducted a systematic benchmarking of multiple architectures 
in a unified fusion framework for medical diagnosis. 
Specific objectives include: 
To develop an end-to-end pipeline for multi-modal MRI-CT 
image fusion using selected deep generative models: Pix2Pix, 
CycleGAN, VAE, β-VAE, and CVAE-GAN. 
To compare the performance of these models across various 
medical imaging datasets (e.g., brain, thoracic, abdominal) 
using quantitative metrics like PSNR, SSIM, and classification 
accuracy. 
To perform ablation studies analyzing the impact of 
architectural variations, training parameters, and loss functions 
on fusion quality. 
To demonstrate real-world clinical applicability through 
case studies, visual examples, and expert validation. 
Significance: 
This study is poised to contribute to both technical innovation 
and clinical practice: 
❖ Technically, it advances the understanding of how different 
generative models behave in image fusion tasks. 
❖ Clinically, it supports the development of AI tools that can 
aid radiologists in diagnosing complex conditions with 
enhanced visual context. 
❖ It also opens doors for future work involving multi-
modality fusion that includes PET, ultrasound, and 
emerging imaging technologies.

Multi-modal image fusion has become integral to contemporary 
radiology workflows because no single modality can capture 
the full spectrum of anatomical and functional information 
required for reliable diagnosis. Magnetic Resonance Imaging 
(MRI) excels at highlighting soft-tissue contrast, while 
Computed Tomography (CT) provides unrivalled bone detail

2.1. 
  Traditional Image Fusion Methods 
Traditional techniques share three core traits:  
❖ deterministic, hand-crafted transformations 
❖ shallow statistical reasoning 
❖ limited capacity for high-order semantic interactions.  
Nevertheless, they laid the technical foundation and still serve 
as competitive baselines. 
2.1.1. 
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) 
PCA projects a pair of registered source images, IMRI and ICT, 
onto an orthogonal eigenbasis (W=w1,w2) derived from the 
covariance matrix ∑=cov(IMRI,ICT). The first principal 
component maximises variance across the joint dataset and is

❖ Strengths. PCA is computationally light, robust to noise 
in small datasets, and guarantees energy compaction (Rui 
et al., 2016). 
❖ Weaknesses. Its linearity fails to model intricate non-
Gaussian dependencies typical of heterogeneous tissues; 
therefore, subtle pathologies, e.g., low-contrast oedema, 
may be suppressed. Moreover, variance is not always 
synonymous with diagnostic salience; a high-variance CT 
artefact (e.g., dental fillings) can dominate the eigenvector 
and distort the output. 
2.1.2. 
  Wavelet Transform (WT) 
Wavelet-based fusion decomposes each source into multi-scale 
sub-bands via the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) using 
mother wavelets such as Daubechies-4 or Symlet-8. Low-
frequency coefficients (approximation) encode gross intensity 
trends, whereas high-frequency coefficients (detail) capture 
edges and texture. Typical fusion rules include 
❖ Maximum Selection: pick the coefficient with larger 
absolute magnitude—good for contrast enhancement. 
❖ Weighted Averaging: learn or heuristically assign weights 
based on local variance or edge entropy. 
❖ Consistency

consistency checks (Li et al., 2019) to reduce artefacts.

Weaknesses. Performance is sensitive to wavelet family, 
decomposition depth, and lacks adaptivity; the same rule is 
applied globally irrespective of organ context. Aliasing 
may arise if shifts between modalities are not sub-pixel

Intensity–Hue–Saturation (IHS): transforms RGB-mapped

❖ Dempster–Shafer Evidence Theory: probabilistically

❖ Joint Bilateral Filtering: builds edge-aware weight maps; 
fails under heavy noise. 
The principal drawback across classical families is their rigidity 
fixed analytic bases cannot fully adapt to the diverse anatomical 
morphologies captured by modern scanners. 
2.2. 
Deep Learning-Based Fusion 
2.2.1. 
Convolutional Neural Networks and Autoencoders 
❖ DenseFuse & FusionNet: Li et al. (2018) replaced static 
wavelets with an encoder–fusion–decoder CNN. Feature 
maps from each modality pass through Dense blocks; 
channel-wise 
L1-norm 
weighting 
selects 
salient 
activations for fusion. The network is optimized with a 
hybrid content loss (pixel MSE) and structure loss (SSIM), 
achieving state-of-the-art mutual information and gradient 
preservation on RIDER Lung CT/MR datasets. 
❖ Residual & Attention Variants: Residual connections 
(He et al., 2016) mitigate vanishing gradients, enabling 
deeper semantic abstraction. FusionDetNet utilises 
Channel Attention (SE-blocks) and Spatial Attention to 
adaptively 
attend 
to 
modality-specific 
cues, 
e.g., 
myelination boundaries in paediatric brain MRIs. These 
CNNs, however, often default to averaging features, thus 
blurring sharp CT edges. 
❖ Autoencoder Families: Sparse AEs enforce L1 penalties 
to emphasise edge-rich components; Denoising AEs learn 
robustness to acquisition noise by reconstructing clean 
fused outputs from synthetically corrupted inputs. Yet, 
pure reconstruction losses produce overly smooth 
images—a problem partially alleviated by adversarial 
critics. 
2.2.2. 
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for 
Cross-domain Fusion 
❖ Pix2Pix & CycleGAN 
Pix2Pix (Isola et al., 2017) learns a conditional mapping  
 
using paired data. The PatchGAN discriminator penalises 
unrealistic local statistics, sharpening micro-calcifications. 
CycleGAN (Zhu et al., 2017) circumvents the scarcity of 
registered pairs by enforcing cycle consistency, allowing 
training on unpaired datasets such as BraTS 2021 MR volumes 
and Head-Neck CT scans. Researchers subsequently added a 
fusion consistency loss to encourage symmetric contribution 
from both modalities (Xu et al., 2023). 
❖ FusionGAN & Dual-Discriminator Architectures 
FusionGAN (Huang et al., 2020) integrates two discriminators: 
DMRI ensures MRI-faithful texture, DCT enforces CT contrast 
realism. The generator is guided by  
▪ 
SSIM loss  
▪ 
Gradient Consistency loss to maintain edge fidelity 
▪ 
Wasserstein distance for stable convergence. Reported 
gains include 2–3 dB PSNR over CycleGAN on the IBSR 
and TCIA datasets. 
❖ WGAN-GP, LSGAN, and Relativistic GANs 
Stabilization strategies include gradient penalty (Gulrajani et 
al., 2017), least-squares loss (Mao et al., 2017), and relativistic 
critics (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2019), which combat mode 
collapse by smoothing the discriminator landscape. In medical 
fusion, WGAN-GP’s Lipschitz constraint exhibits superior 
convergence under limited batch sizes (often ≤ 8 due to GPU 
memory), critical for 3-D volumes. 
❖ Transformer-Augmented GANs 
Recent works embed cross-modal attention transformers 
within the generator, enabling global context sharing between 
MRI T2-Flair lesions and CT haemorrhage patterns. Swin-
UNet-GAN reached 0.94 Dice on ischaemic core segmentation 
post-fusion (Chen et al., 2024).

Limitations in Existing Approaches

Despite remarkable gains, several persistent obstacles prevent 
widespread clinical integration. 
2.3.1. 
Loss of Resolution and Semantic Detail 
High-resolution 512×512×N volumes challenge GPU memory; 
many studies down-sample to 256², inadvertently discarding 
micro-tumour signatures (< 3 mm). Even full-resolution GANs 
may introduce checker-board artefacts due to transposed 
convolutions. Super-resolution post-processing helps but adds 
latency. 
Moreover, feature dominance skews fused intensity. When 
CT’s high-frequency bone edges dominate the discriminator’s 
gradient, subtle MRI T2 hyperintensities risk suppression, 
potentially masking early demyelinating lesions. Multi-
objective loss weighting is still heuristic, often tuned via grid 
search. 
2.3.2. 
Mode Collapse and Training Instability in GANs 
Mode collapse remains acute under imbalanced class 
distributions—e.g., abundant healthy slices vs. scarce 
pathological 
slices. 
Techniques 
like 
mini-batch 
discrimination and spectral normalisation partially alleviate 
the problem, yet require meticulous hyperparameter tuning. 
Instability is compounded by 3-D data: Generators employ 
volumetric convolutions that explode parameter counts, 
slowing feedback loops and exacerbating non-convergence. 
Curriculum learning (progressive layer-unfreezing) has been 
proposed but with limited reproducibility across centres. 
2.3.3. 
Interpretability and Trustworthiness 
Clinicians demand causal insight: Which pixels originated 
predominantly from MRI?  Why did the network prioritise one 
modality over the other at a given voxel?  Current saliency 
tools, Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, are ill-suited for fusion 
because the modalities enter as concatenated channels rather 
than separate paths. Without transparent attribution, regulatory 
approval (e.g., FDA 510(k)) is unlikely. 
2.3.4. 
Cross-Modality Registration Errors 
Rigid/aligned slices are assumed in nearly all fusion networks, 
but small rotational offsets (1–2 °) or respiratory motion (≈ 3 
mm) are common in abdominal studies. Mis-registration leads 
to ghost edges and blunted vessel walls. While Spatial 
Transformer Networks (STN) can correct minor shifts, they 
struggle with non-linear deformations typical in thoracic 
imaging. 
2.3.5. 
Data Scarcity and Domain Shift 
Annotated paired MRI-CT datasets with voxel-wise ground 
truth remain scarce. Public repositories (BraTS, TCIA) cover 
primarily neuro-oncology, leaving thoracic, abdominal, and 
pediatric domains underrepresented. Domain shift scanner 
vendors, acquisition protocols, and slice thickness—cause 
performance drop when deploying to external hospitals. Few 
studies employ domain-generalisation tricks such as style 
randomization or adversarial feature alignment. 
2.3.6. 
Computational Burden and Real-Time Constraints 
Although edge-optimised models exist (TensorRT, FP16 
quantisation), 3-D GANs still require > 40 ms per slice on an 
NVIDIA A100—acceptable for offline reading but prohibitive 
for intra-operative navigation, where ≤ 10 ms latency is 
preferred. Hardware-agnostic optimisation frameworks (TVM, 
OpenVINO) are under-utilised in the literature. 
4.4  Synthesis and Research Gap 
The survey reveals a gap between algorithmic sophistication 
and clinical viability. Classical techniques fail to capture non-
linear cross-modal semantics, whereas current deep generative 
models excel in visual realism but labour under training 
instability, opacity, and computational overhead. No consensus 
exists on a standardised evaluation protocol; reported metrics 
vary from simple PSNR to task-driven metrics like Dice for 
tumour segmentation, hindering fair comparison. 
Hence, this study proposes:  
❖ a hybrid CVAE-WGAN architecture with disentangled 
latent conditioning to balance sharpness and uncertainty 
estimation,  
❖ a multi-scale perceptual-gradient loss to prevent MRI or 
CT dominance,  
❖ an explainability module using cross-modal Shapley 
value decomposition, and comprehensive benchmarking 
on four anatomically diverse datasets with identical pre-
processing 
pipelines. 
Addressing 
the 
highlighted 
limitations positions the proposed framework to advance 
multi-modal fusion toward reliable bedside deployment. 
3. Methodology  
The methodology for this study is centered on designing, 
training, and evaluating deep generative models—specifically 
GANs and VAEs—for fusing MRI and CT images. The 
objective is to leverage the complementary strengths of both 
modalities to enhance diagnostic precision through pixel- and 
feature-level fusion. This section details the data acquisition 
process, network architecture, fusion strategy, and training 
pipeline. 
3.1 Data Acquisition 
3.1.1 Dataset Selection 
Two widely used public datasets were selected for this study: 
BraTS (Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge): This dataset 
provides multimodal MRI scans (T1, T2, FLAIR, and post-
contrast T1-Gd) from patients with glioblastoma and low-grade 
glioma. While CT images are not inherently included, they were 
simulated or registered from external sources for multimodal 
fusion purposes. 
TCIA (The Cancer Imaging Archive): Specifically, the 
"Head-Neck Cetuximab" and "Lung-PET-CT-Dx" datasets 
were utilized, providing aligned MRI and CT scans from 
oncology cases. 
3.1.2 Preprocessing Steps 
MRI and CT images inherently differ in intensity distributions, 
resolution, and contrast. To prepare them for fusion:

❖ Intensity Normalization: Each MRI and CT scan was 
normalized to a common intensity scale using z-score 
normalization (mean = 0, std = 1). 
❖ Registration: Non-rigid image registration using mutual 
information was employed to spatially align MRI and CT 
images. 
❖ Resizing and Cropping: All images were resized to a 
uniform dimension of 256×256 pixels. Regions of interest 
(e.g., tumor sites) were centered using bounding box 
extraction. 
❖ Noise Filtering: A median filter was applied to reduce salt-
and-pepper noise. 
❖ Contrast Enhancement: CLAHE (Contrast Limited 
Adaptive Histogram Equalization) was used to improve 
local contrast in MRI images. 
3.2 Network Architecture Design 
The image fusion system was built using two classes of 
generative models: 
3.2.1 Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) 
Two GAN variants were explored: 
❖ Pix2Pix GAN: A conditional GAN model suitable for 
paired data. It uses a U-Net generator with skip connections 
and a PatchGAN discriminator to learn fine-grained pixel-
level mappings between MRI and CT images. The 
generator receives a concatenated MRI-CT pair and learns 
to output a fused image. 
❖ CycleGAN: Used when aligned paired data is unavailable. 
CycleGAN performs unpaired image-to-image translation 
and includes two generators and two discriminators, with 
cycle-consistency loss to preserve semantic structure. 
CycleGAN helped learn CT-to-MRI mappings that support 
fusion in the absence of registration. 
3.2.2 Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) 
The following VAE models were implemented: 
❖ Standard 
VAE: 
Comprises 
an 
encoder-decoder 
architecture with a Gaussian latent space. MRI and CT 
images are encoded into latent vectors and decoded into a 
fused representation. 
❖ β-VAE: A variant that introduces a β coefficient to the KL 
divergence term in the VAE loss function, promoting 
disentangled latent representations. This helped separate 
anatomical features (from CT) and functional patterns 
(from MRI). 
❖ Conditional VAE (CVAE): Introduced conditional inputs 
(modality type) into the encoding process to guide 
generation toward specific fused outputs. This model 
improved semantic fidelity in multi-organ imaging. 
Each model was constructed using PyTorch with GPU 
acceleration and batch normalization. 
3.3 Fusion Strategy 
Fusion was approached from both feature-level and pixel-level 
strategies to evaluate their comparative advantages. 
3.3.1 Feature-Level Fusion 
❖ CNN Encoder Fusion: Features were extracted from 
intermediate convolutional layers of both MRI and CT 
images and concatenated along the depth axis. These were 
then decoded into a single fused image using a transposed 
convolutional decoder. 
❖ Attention-Based Fusion: An attention module was 
introduced to learn weighted importance across features 
extracted from both modalities. Soft attention maps 
allowed the network to emphasize tumor boundaries from 
MRI and bone structures from CT. 
3.3.2 Pixel-Level Fusion 
❖ Linear Pixel Averaging: A baseline fusion approach 
where each pixel in the fused image is the weighted 
average of MRI and CT pixel values. 
❖ GAN-Based Pixel Fusion: The generator learns a direct 
pixel-wise transformation that blends MRI and CT content 
based on adversarial and perceptual feedback. 
❖ VAE 
Reconstruction-Based 
Fusion:

representations were merged and decoded into pixel-
domain fused outputs, effectively learning anatomical and

4.2 Baseline Comparisons 
To fairly assess the improvements offered by deep generative 
models, this study implemented and compared both classical 
and contemporary baseline methods for multi-modal image 
fusion. This provided a comprehensive benchmark that 
highlights the performance gap between traditional techniques 
and learning-based approaches. 
4.2.1 Classical Image Fusion Methods 
Three popular and historically significant traditional fusion 
methods were implemented: 
❖ Principal Component Analysis (PCA): A statistical 
method that fuses MRI and CT by extracting principal 
components 
and 
retaining 
the 
most 
significant 
eigenvectors. Although computationally light, it often 
suppresses minor but diagnostically critical details like 
lesion boundaries. 
❖ Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT): Both images were 
decomposed into wavelet sub-bands (LL, LH, HL, HH), 
and fused coefficients were reconstructed based on 
maximum energy rules. While DWT is effective at 
preserving frequency information, it suffers from limited 
edge localization. 
❖ Laplacian Pyramid Fusion: Used multi-resolution 
decomposition to extract low-frequency and high-
frequency details at various scales. This method is sensitive 
to misregistration and often introduces ringing artifacts in 
the fused output. 
Each classical method served as a reference to evaluate 
improvements in visual fidelity, diagnostic accuracy, and 
boundary preservation when compared to deep learning-based 
models. 
4.2.2 Deep Learning Baselines 
The following deep learning models were considered as strong 
contemporary baselines: 
❖ Autoencoder-Based Fusion: Separate encoders were 
trained for MRI and CT, and fused feature vectors were 
decoded into a synthetic composite image. This model 
performed well in preserving global structure but lacked 
fine-grain control over specific feature fusion. 
❖ UNet-Fusion: Adapted from UNet’s encoder-decoder 
architecture, the model was trained to merge inputs at each 
scale via skip connections. Useful in segmentation-rich 
applications, this model was limited by over-smoothing 
effects during reconstruction. 
❖ Residual Network Fusion (ResNet-Fusion): Utilized 
residual blocks to enhance spatial fidelity in the fusion 
process, particularly effective for preserving anatomical 
edges. However, it lacked flexibility in capturing modality-
specific texture variations. 
These models were trained using the same datasets and 
evaluation metrics to provide a robust comparison against the 
primary models of interest: Pix2Pix GAN, CycleGAN, VAE, 
β-VAE, and CVAE-GAN.

4.3 Validation Process 
Model validation is essential for evaluating generalizability, 
reliability, and clinical readiness. This section details the 
methods used to validate fusion model performance across 
quantitative and qualitative dimensions. 
4.3.1 K-Fold Cross-Validation 
To mitigate overfitting and maximize dataset utilization, a 5-
fold cross-validation approach was employed: 
❖ The entire dataset was randomly partitioned into 5 equal 
subsets. 
❖ Each model was trained on 4 folds and tested on the 
remaining fold, iterating this process five times to cover all 
data splits. 
❖ For each run, metrics such as Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio 
(PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and 
classification accuracy (on tumor classification using a pre-
trained ResNet50) were recorded. 
❖ The average and standard deviation of each metric were 
computed to represent model performance. 
This approach ensured that no image was used both for training 
and testing within the same fold and helped to reduce 
performance bias from data split selection. 
4.3.2 Ground Truth Generation 
One of the major challenges in image fusion evaluation is the 
lack of a definitive ground truth. This study addressed this 
limitation through a combination of expert annotation and 
synthetic simulation: 
A. Manual Expert Annotation 
❖ A team of three board-certified radiologists was recruited 
to annotate MRI and CT images independently. 
❖ Regions of interest (ROIs) such as tumors, edema, and 
structural boundaries were outlined using annotation tools 
like ITK-SNAP and 3D Slicer. 
❖ Discrepancies were resolved through consensus meetings, 
and agreement levels were measured using inter-observer 
Dice coefficient scores (>0.85). 
B. Consensus-Based Fusion Labels 
❖ Annotations from both modalities were fused using 
majority voting, weighted interpolation, and confidence 
maps to create reference composite masks. 
❖ These masks served as pseudo-ground truth to evaluate the 
structural correctness and feature retention in the fused 
images. 
C. Synthetic Ground Truth 
❖ Synthetic fusion tasks were also simulated using generated 
anatomical phantoms and embedded patterns. 
❖ Known structures and pathologies (e.g., synthetic tumors 
with Gaussian profiles) were added into MRI or CT scans 
separately and fused using models. This allowed ground-
truth image fusion with perfect knowledge of the inputs. 
The combined use of real-world expert annotations and 
controlled synthetic data ensured a reliable evaluation 
framework across a range of diagnostic scenarios.

6. Discussion 
6.1 GANs vs. VAEs in Medical Image Fusion 
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational 
Autoencoders (VAEs) each present unique strengths and 
limitations in the context of medical image fusion, particularly 
for combining multi-modal inputs such as MRI and CT scans. 
GAN-based fusion excels in generating highly realistic and 
visually coherent outputs. The adversarial training setup allows 
GANs to learn fine structural details and high-frequency 
content, which is crucial when fusing medical images for tasks 
like tumor boundary detection or organ delineation. Techniques 
like Pix2Pix or CycleGAN have shown strong performance in 
synthesizing realistic cross-modal representations by learning 
pixel-level correspondences and texture translation between CT 
and MRI domains. For example, CycleGAN avoids the need for 
perfectly aligned paired datasets, allowing unsupervised 
learning of mappings between modalities. However, GANs can 
be unstable during training, with problems like mode collapse, 
where the generator produces limited diversity, potentially 
omitting vital diagnostic features. 
In contrast, VAE-based fusion emphasizes probabilistic 
modeling and latent space regularization. VAEs are particularly 
valuable 
for 
learning 
compressed, 
structured 
latent 
representations of multi-modal medical data. In applications 
such as organ classification, anomaly detection, or feature-level 
fusion, VAEs offer strong generalization through their ability 
to sample diverse yet consistent outputs from learned 
distributions. Variants like β-VAE and CVAE-GAN allow for 
controlled and disentangled representation learning, which is 
advantageous in identifying subtle differences across imaging 
modalities. Nevertheless, VAEs often suffer from blurry 
image reconstruction due to their tendency to optimize a 
lower-bound approximation of the likelihood, which can 
diminish fine anatomical detail something critical in high-
resolution diagnostics. 
Fusion performance comparison (from our results) suggests 
that CVAE-GAN hybrid models combine the realism of GANs 
with the stability of VAEs, outperforming standalone models in 
both accuracy and image fidelity. 
6.2 Interpretability, Generalization, and Explainability 
Despite their power, deep generative models, especially GANs, 
are often considered black boxes in clinical settings. 
Interpretability is critical in healthcare, where radiologists and 
physicians must trust and understand how a fused image was 
generated and what features were emphasized or suppressed. 
VAEs offer a slight advantage in interpretability, as their 
probabilistic formulation and latent space allow for 
introspection—one can inspect latent vectors and assess how 
different components contribute to the final fused image. 
Disentangled latent spaces in β-VAEs can be linked to specific 
anatomical features or modality-specific traits. 
GANs, however, are less interpretable. While saliency maps 
and attention mechanisms can be applied to GAN-based 
outputs, they often do not offer the same level of semantic 
traceability. This becomes problematic when the fused image 
introduces hallucinated structures that may not exist in either 
input modality—raising concerns for false-positive or false-
negative diagnoses. 
In terms of generalization, models trained on high-resolution 
and balanced datasets, such as TCIA or BraTS, show robust 
performance. But across institutions with varying imaging 
protocols, models may fail to generalize. Domain adaptation 
techniques or domain-invariant feature learning are required but 
still underexplored in medical image fusion. 
Explainability remains a frontier. Integration of Explainable 
AI (XAI) frameworks, such as LIME or SHAP, tailored for 
image fusion tasks, is essential for future adoption in clinical 
workflows. 
6.3 Limitations of the Current Study 
While our experiments demonstrate promising results, several 
limitations must be acknowledged: 
❖ Modality Alignment: MRI and CT images, though often 
taken from the same patient, may be misaligned spatially 
and temporally. Even with rigid and non-rigid registration 
techniques, perfect alignment is rarely achievable, leading 
to potential artifacts or misleading fused outputs. GANs, in 
particular, can exaggerate these discrepancies if not 
properly regularized. 
❖ Dataset Imbalance: The number of available datasets that 
contain both MRI and CT images for the same patients is 
limited. Many public datasets focus exclusively on a single 
modality. This restricts the diversity of training data and 
introduces a bias towards the dominant modality or class. 
In our study, tumors and brain structures were 
overrepresented compared to other organ systems, which 
might affect the generalizability of our conclusions across 
broader diagnostic applications. 
❖ Evaluation Metrics: Metrics such as SSIM, PSNR, and 
even accuracy, while helpful, do not always reflect clinical 
relevance. A fused image may score high on image quality 
metrics but still miss critical pathologies, or vice versa. 
Therefore, human-in-the-loop validation with radiologist

6.4 Ethical and Clinical Considerations 
As with all applications of AI in medicine, there are ethical, 
legal, and clinical implications to consider in multi-modal 
image fusion: 
❖ Diagnostic Reliability: Automated fusion may introduce 
structures not originally present, particularly with GAN 
hallucinations. If undetected, this can lead to misdiagnosis, 
overtreatment, or missed treatment opportunities. Human 
oversight must remain integral, with fused images serving 
as supplementary tools, not replacements. 
❖ Data Privacy: The use of centralized medical datasets may 
violate patient confidentiality if not handled properly. 
While federated learning offers a solution, it is not yet 
standard in fusion tasks. Models must be trained with strict 
HIPAA/GDPR-compliant protocols, and synthetic data 
generation must avoid re-identifiability. 
❖ Equity and Accessibility: There is a risk of creating 
healthcare disparity if fusion-based diagnostic tools are 
only available in well-funded hospitals or developed 
countries. Models trained exclusively on high-quality, 
Western datasets may underperform in LMIC contexts due 
to imaging protocol differences or population variances.

Abstract: Medical imaging plays a pivotal role in early disease detection, surgical planning, and post-treatment monitoring. Among various imaging modalities, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT) are widely used due to their complementary strengths MRI offers superior soft tissue contrast, while CT excels in visualizing dense structures like bones. However, relying on a single modality often limits diagnostic precision, especially in complex clinical cases such as brain tumors, stroke evaluation, and orthopedic planning. Consequently, fusing information from both MRI and CT images into a unified representation, known as multi-modal image fusion, has become an essential approach to enhance diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision-making. Traditional image fusion techniques, including wavelet transforms, PCA, and Laplacian pyramids, have demonstrated limited performance due to their reliance on handcrafted features and linear transformations. These methods often result in loss of critical structural or functional information. The rise of deep learning, particularly Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), has revolutionized image processing by enabling the automatic extraction and synthesis of complex features across domains. These generative models not only learn hierarchical representations from data but also preserve the contextual integrity of both modalities during the fusion process. GANs have shown exceptional capability in generating realistic, high-resolution images, while VAEs offer probabilistic latent space modeling that is beneficial for uncertainty estimation in medical contexts. This study proposes and evaluates a multi-modal image fusion framework leveraging GAN and VAE architectures to combine MRI and CT images for enhanced medical diagnosis. The research utilizes multiple publicly available datasets (e.g., TCIA, BraTS), implements both pixel-level and feature-level fusion strategies, and conducts extensive evaluations using quantitative metrics such as Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and classification accuracy for downstream diagnostic tasks. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed GAN- and VAE-based fusion models significantly outperform traditional fusion techniques in terms of visual clarity, preservation of diagnostic details, and computational efficiency. Moreover, a comprehensive benchmark of different model variants (Pix2Pix, CycleGAN, β-VAE, CVAE-GAN) is provided to guide future research and clinical implementation. This work contributes to the field by offering a reproducible framework, open-source implementation, and actionable insights for integrating deep generative models into radiological workflows, thereby paving the way for AI-augmented precision diagnostics.
